# Paper Plaine

> arXiv research papers explained in plain English, updated twice daily.

## What this site is

Paper Plaine surfaces fresh academic research from Cornell University's arXiv preprint database and translates it into plain English for general audiences. Every paper gets three things: a plain-language subtitle (8–12 words capturing the core idea), a 2–3 sentence summary leading with what was found, and a "why it matters" explanation focused on real-world consequences.

The site currently has 1213 papers in its archive across 9 subject areas: AI, Computer Science, Physics, Mathematics, Biology, Finance, Statistics, Engineering, Economics. New papers are added automatically twice daily (7 AM and 7 PM UTC). Only first-version arXiv submissions from the past 30 days are considered. Papers are scored for quality signals: venue acceptance (NeurIPS, ICML, Nature, PNAS, etc.), cross-disciplinary listings, and appropriate length.

## How content is structured

Each paper entry contains:
- Formal arXiv title and authors
- Plain-English subtitle — a one-phrase translation of the paper's core idea
- Summary — 2–3 sentences leading with the finding, not the method
- Why it matters — real-world consequences, stated directly
- Link to the full paper on arXiv
- Category and posting date

## Site structure

- Home / archive: https://paperplaine.com (paginated, 12 papers per page)
- Per-category pages: https://paperplaine.com/<category-slug>
- Per-paper pages: https://paperplaine.com/papers/<slug>
- RSS feed: https://paperplaine.com/feed.xml
- llms.txt (this file): https://paperplaine.com/llms.txt
- llms-full.txt (full text of recent papers): https://paperplaine.com/llms-full.txt
- Sitemap: https://paperplaine.com/sitemap.xml

## 10 most recent papers

### Deneb-Vritra: Descriptions, Edges and Names Examined by Blocking Via Restoring Token Representations and Attention
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/deneb-vritra-descriptions-edges
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Mohammed Nayeem Khan, Akhil P, Shahina Shaik
- arXiv: 2611.31139
- Plain-English subtitle: How AI models choose answers by name rather than meaning
- Summary: Researchers found that a 421-million-parameter AI model often picks the wrong answer when the correct option's name is swapped onto another option's description—choosing based on the name alone 53–67% of the time. By blocking specific neural pathways in layers 14–17, they cut this "name shortcut" down to 11–16% while keeping overall accuracy at 90%, pinpointing exactly where the model abandons semantic reasoning for label matching.
- Why it matters: AI systems deployed for high-stakes tasks like medical diagnosis or legal review need to actually reason about content, not just match labels. This work reveals a blind spot in current models: they can be tricked into ignoring meaning entirely, and shows engineers exactly which neural circuits to audit and retrain to close the gap. Understanding these shortcuts is essential before trusting AI with decisions that require real comprehension.

### Exact Volume-Preserving Diffeomorphic Shear Splitting: Continuous-Discrete Geometric Bounds, Reversible Memory Backpropagation, and Expressivity Frontiers in Volumetric Mapping
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/exact-volume-preserving-diffeomorphic
- Category: Engineering
- Authors: Alvaro Garcia-Casas
- arXiv: 2611.31343
- Plain-English subtitle: A new way to map organs while perfectly preserving their volume
- Summary: Researchers developed a method for registering medical images—aligning one scan to another—that maintains exact volume preservation at machine precision while running 2–4 times faster than standard approaches. By decomposing the deformation into simple shear operations that have known mathematical solutions, the method eliminates numerical errors that plague existing techniques and reduces GPU memory use by 78%.
- Why it matters: Medical imaging relies on comparing scans across time or between patients, and errors in that comparison can compound during diagnosis or surgery planning. This method guarantees that tissue volumes stay exactly correct—no artificial shrinkage or expansion—while consuming far less computing power. For cardiac and brain imaging, this means faster, more reliable registration without the numerical artifacts that can mask real disease or create false positives.

### A colored look at anyons and parastatistics
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/a-colored-look-at
- Category: Physics
- Authors: Francesco Toppan
- arXiv: 2611.31841
- Plain-English subtitle: A new mathematical lens for understanding exotic particle behavior
- Summary: Physicists have shown that a 40-year-old generalization of algebra called color Lie algebras naturally describes two types of unusual particles: paraparticles (which can exist anywhere in space) and anyons (which can only exist in two dimensions). This framework doesn't just fit these particles into existing theory—it reveals new physical signatures that distinguish different kinds of parastatistics.
- Why it matters: Anyons and paraparticles are more than theoretical curiosities; they appear in exotic materials and quantum systems that physicists are actively trying to engineer for quantum computers and advanced electronics. Having the right mathematical language makes it clearer which exotic particles can actually exist in a given physical system, and what measurable differences to look for when searching for them in experiments.

### CTLink: A Text-Prompted Segmentation Model for Linking Radiology Report Findings to 3D Chest CT Scans
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/ctlink-a-text-prompted
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Mohammed Baharoon, Sung Eun Kim, Mahmoud Hussain Alabbad et al.
- arXiv: 2611.31222
- Plain-English subtitle: Teaching AI to highlight what radiologists describe in chest scan reports
- Summary: A new AI system called CTLink can pinpoint abnormalities in chest CT scans by reading the radiologist's written report—automatically drawing boxes around the exact locations of findings like nodules or fluid that doctors mention only in text. On a major benchmark, CTLink outperformed existing tools by a large margin, achieving 81.6% accuracy at locating reported findings and matching the consistency of two independent radiologists reviewing the same scans.
- Why it matters: Radiologists currently must manually review both the written report and the scan to verify findings match up, which is time-consuming and error-prone. CTLink automates that linking process, letting radiologists instantly see visual confirmation of each finding they report—catching mismatches, reducing re-reading time, and making it harder for important abnormalities to slip through unnoticed. The system is accurate enough to match inter-radiologist agreement, suggesting it could be deployed in routine clinical workflows without sacrificing reliability.

### Towards Edge Artificial Intelligence for Predicting Antimicrobial Resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/towards-edge-artificial-intelligence
- Category: Quantitative Biology
- Authors: Nishat Tasnim, Faisal Ahmed, Rokan Uddin Faruqui
- arXiv: 2611.29143
- Plain-English subtitle: Running TB drug-resistance tests on hospital computers in poor countries
- Summary: Researchers developed a lightweight machine learning system that predicts whether tuberculosis bacteria are resistant to antibiotics by analyzing their genetic code—and it runs on basic hospital computers rather than requiring expensive supercomputers. The system correctly identified drug resistance patterns about 82% of the time across 20 different antibiotics, making it practical for clinics in low-income countries where advanced computing infrastructure doesn't exist.
- Why it matters: Doctors in hospitals across Africa and Asia could get same-day answers about which drugs will actually work against a patient's TB infection, instead of waiting days or weeks for results from distant labs—or guessing and prescribing ineffective treatments that worsen drug resistance. This speed matters enormously: resistant TB already kills hundreds of thousands yearly, and faster diagnosis directly shortens treatment delays and reduces the spread of untreatable strains.

### Marked INAR model and the rough Hawkes--Heston limit
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/marked-inar-model-and
- Category: Quantitative Finance
- Authors: Xiaoyu Wang, Yingli Wang, Lingjiong Zhu
- arXiv: 2611.29565
- Plain-English subtitle: A faster way to price options in markets with sudden jumps
- Summary: Researchers developed a computational method that can price financial options in markets where volatility and price jumps happen together—a scenario that's mathematically complex but realistic. The algorithm runs roughly 100 times faster than naive approaches while still converging to theoretically correct values, with tests showing implied volatility curves matching established benchmarks across different market conditions.
- Why it matters: Options traders and risk managers need to price derivatives quickly and accurately, especially in turbulent markets where traditional models break down. This algorithm cuts computation time dramatically without sacrificing precision, making real-time pricing feasible for institutions that currently rely on slower approximations or less realistic market models.

### Ego-HMB: Human Motion Bridging from Egocentric Images via A Motion Bridge Diffusion Model
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/ego-hmb-human-motion
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Gaoge Han, Yongkang Cheng, Shaoli Huang et al.
- arXiv: 2611.29218
- Plain-English subtitle: Filling in the motion gap between two first-person video frames
- Summary: Researchers created an AI system that generates realistic human motion sequences from two first-person camera images taken seconds apart—the kind of footage from VR headsets or body cameras. The system outperforms simpler methods by learning endpoint poses and smooth motion together in a single unified model, rather than solving each problem separately.
- Why it matters: VR/AR systems and robots need to understand and predict human movement from first-person camera feeds, but existing methods require clean 3D pose data that wearables can't provide. This approach works directly from raw video frames, making motion prediction practical for devices people actually wear, which could improve everything from gesture recognition in VR to robots that work safely alongside humans.

### Ziv Meets Sumcheck: Zero-Knowledge Proofs of Floating-Point LLM Inference
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/ziv-meets-sumcheck-zero
- Category: Computer Science
- Authors: Hassan Khodaiemehr, Khadijeh Bagheri, Chen Feng
- arXiv: 2611.29188
- Plain-English subtitle: Proving AI models work correctly without revealing their secrets
- Summary: Researchers created a system to mathematically prove that a language model like GPT-2 produced a specific output without exposing the model itself — and crucially, they did it using the actual floating-point arithmetic that runs on real computers, not simplified approximations. They proved GPT-2 small's entire forward pass in 19 minutes, with verification taking just 21 seconds, and the system rejected all 236 attempted attacks.
- Why it matters: Organizations could verify that an AI system is working correctly and hasn't been tampered with, without having to trust the company running it or give away proprietary model details. This matters for high-stakes applications like medical diagnosis or financial decisions, where you need proof a model isn't lying or manipulating outputs — and it now works on the actual arithmetic these systems use in production, not just theoretical toy versions.

### Optimal isotropic three-material conducting composites with an ideal conductor, in the plane and in space.Bounds and optimal structures
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/optimal-isotropic-three-material
- Category: Mathematics
- Authors: Andrej Cherkaev, Leonid Gibiansky
- arXiv: 2611.29235
- Plain-English subtitle: Finding the perfect blend of three materials to block heat as much as possible
- Summary: Researchers solved a century-old puzzle in materials science: what arrangement of three conducting materials—including one that conducts perfectly—minimizes heat flow through a composite? They proved that the optimal structure consists of nested spheres with wrapped layers, and derived mathematical formulas predicting exactly how well any such arrangement can perform based on material properties and how much of each material you use.
- Why it matters: This framework helps engineers design better insulators and thermal barriers for everything from aerospace to electronics. The mathematical bounds reveal fundamental limits on what any three-material system can achieve, so manufacturers know whether they're building something close to ideal or whether a different material combination might work better. The constructive proof also provides a practical recipe for arranging materials to reach those theoretical limits.

### Communication-Efficient Federated Learning of Latent Patient Representations from Multi-Institutional EHRs
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/communication-efficient-federated-learning
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Zhiyu Yan, Shiao Liu, Rahul Mahajan et al.
- arXiv: 2611.27900
- Plain-English subtitle: Learning patient patterns from multiple hospitals without sharing sensitive records
- Summary: Researchers developed a method that lets hospitals collaborate on identifying patient subgroups from electronic health records while keeping individual patient data private and minimizing data transfer between sites. Applied to stroke patients across multiple facilities, the approach recovered the same patient patterns that would emerge from pooling all records directly, while each hospital shared only aggregate statistics and mathematical summaries instead of raw patient information.
- Why it matters: Hospitals often can't combine patient records due to privacy rules and technical barriers, which means insights are trapped in silos and patterns learned at one hospital may not apply elsewhere. This method lets institutions participate in collaborative research without breaking privacy agreements or overwhelming networks with massive file transfers—making it practical for hospitals to build better diagnostic tools and treatment strategies that work across diverse patient populations.
